title: Does Loving Someone Give You the Right to Know Everything About Them?
deck: Intimacy requires knowing what matters, but trust does not mean making someone’s entire inner life public.
body: Intimacy often brings a wish with it: I want to know everything about you.

Where you went, whom you spoke to, why you suddenly fell silent, what you are really thinking. The more we know, the closer we seem to be; whatever we have not been told is easily understood as a barrier, or even a betrayal.
Love is thus sometimes recast as a comprehensive right to know.
“If you trust me, why can’t you tell me?”
This sounds reasonable, because concealment can indeed harm a relationship.

When two people’s lives are connected, some facts directly change the other person’s choices. Shared risks, commitments already made, and important information affecting the other person’s body, finances, or future plans cannot be treated merely as personal secrets.
If someone holds facts that could change the other person’s decision but lets them continue to consent without knowing, what is being preserved is more than private space.
The conditions under which the other person chooses have also been altered.
But not everything left unsaid is this kind of concealment.

A person can still have feelings they have not yet sorted out, keep memories they do not intend to share, and develop a thought without an audience. They need not submit every hesitation, every fleeting thought, and every period of solitude to the relationship for review.
Intimacy makes people willing to open many doors, but it does not mean that every door loses its lock from then on.
Sometimes we want to know everything not because the facts themselves matter, but because not knowing unsettles us.

Gaps leave room for imagination. We worry about being excluded, about the other person having a world that no longer needs us, and about being unable to protect the relationship if we cannot predict what will happen.
So we demand more information, hoping to exchange transparency for security.
But transparency cannot eliminate uncertainty altogether.

Even knowing every journey and every conversation cannot give us complete possession of another person’s understanding. A sentence they speak may still contain something not yet formed in their mind; the account they give of themselves today may change tomorrow.
Between people there will always be places that cannot be opened up completely.
This is not necessarily a flaw in the relationship. It simply means the other person is not a file that can be fully grasped once we have enough information.
Real trust therefore cannot rest solely on “I know everything.”

It also includes this: even if I do not know every change within you, I still trust you to tell me what genuinely affects me; even if you have space of your own, I do not automatically interpret that space as a rejection of me.
Of course, “This is private” cannot be a universal way to avoid responsibility either.
A simple distinction may help:
Does this matter belong only to your inner life, or would it change whether another person is willing to keep making the same choice?
The former may be kept private. The latter usually needs to be explained.

You need not report every thought. But if something that has already happened would make the other person reconsider a commitment, they have a right to know before continuing. You can have relationships and space of your own, but if arrangements within them cross boundaries both of you have explicitly agreed on, personal freedom alone cannot account for that.
Love gives no one an unlimited right to inspect another person, nor does it allow the other person to use secrets to take away real choices in a shared life.
Both boundaries must hold at the same time.
Sometimes sharing loses its original meaning because it is demanded.

Someone might have been willing to speak gradually about a vulnerable experience. But when the other person insists, “You have to tell me now,” sharing changes from trust into proof. They no longer speak because they want to draw closer, but to avoid suspicion.
Such transparency may increase information without increasing intimacy.
Real intimacy is more than knowing a great deal.

It also appears when someone can say, “I don’t want to talk about this yet,” and the other person can ask whether it affects shared decisions, receive a clear answer, and still allow that door to remain closed for now.
Loving someone is not acquiring ownership of their entire inner world.

It means carefully distinguishing which facts are conditions of our shared life and which spaces still belong to them alone; which silences take away my choices and which simply remind me that they always have a life in which I cannot take their place.
A relationship that can allow this may lack the sense of certainty that absolute transparency brings.
But it preserves a more important kind of trust: we can draw close to one another without first having to surrender ourselves completely.
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
